article.title: Adiponectin and progression from impaired fasting glucose in community care
article.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adipose-derived signals may help distinguish people whose mildly elevated glucose will progress, but prospective evidence from routine community care remains limited. We asked whether baseline adiponectin predicts progression to diabetes in people with prediabetes. Adiponectin was considered an adipose-derived hormone in this investigation.
METHODS: The prospective cohort followed 638 adults with prediabetes recruited through community clinics, using adiponectin measured at entry to define the exposure.
METHODS: Cox regression related diabetes onset to a doubling of baseline adiponectin during four years of observation.
METHODS: Diabetes required confirmation at a repeat visit, and staff recorded medication changes alongside the scheduled clinical assessments.
RESULTS: Higher baseline adiponectin was associated with significantly lower incidence of diabetes (hazard ratio 0.76; 95% CI 0.62–0.93; p=0.008).
RESULTS: During surveillance, 96 participants developed diabetes; the median baseline adiponectin concentration was 6.8 [4.9–9.1] micrograms/mL.
RESULTS: An additional exploratory model linked higher adiponectin to a smaller increase in waist circumference, with a slope of −0.7 cm per doubling (p=0.04), although that analysis was not corrected for multiple testing.
CONCLUSIONS: The biomarker identified a gradient of subsequent glycaemic risk within people who already had impaired glucose regulation.
CONCLUSIONS: Whether repeated measurement adds useful information to inexpensive clinical prediction tools should be tested before a screening role is proposed.

article.title: Circulating adiponectin precedes diabetes onset in primary care
article.abstract:
Prediction of metabolic deterioration is difficult when fasting glucose is only modestly raised, prompting interest in hormones that reflect adipose tissue function. Our objective was to relate entry adiponectin concentrations to diabetes diagnosed during primary care follow-up. The exposure of interest was adiponectin, an adipose-derived hormone.
Adults with prediabetes entered a prospective cohort through prevention services and returned for assessments over five years.
The risk analysis used a Cox model with adiponectin expressed per doubling; repeat testing distinguished a new diagnosis from an isolated abnormal measurement.
Participants continued their usual care while attending surveillance visits, with laboratory records checked independently against the diagnosis register.
Greater adiponectin at entry was associated with lower diabetes risk.
There were 113 incident cases, and the mean age at entry was 57 ± 8 years; participants who returned for all visits had slightly lower waist measurements than those missing a visit.
For a secondary outcome, the coefficient relating adiponectin to change in fasting insulin was −0.4 mU/L per doubling (P = .09).
These observations place adiponectin upstream of clinically detected diabetes but do not demonstrate that increasing the hormone prevents disease.
External validation and evaluation of measurement costs would be needed before this association could justify adding another test to primary care surveillance.

article.title: Sex-specific chemerin associations in metabolic syndrome
article.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Chemerin has been proposed as a link between inflammatory signalling and impaired insulin action, but averaging across sexes may conceal clinically useful differences. We investigated whether chemerin associations with insulin resistance differ between women and men. Chemerin was examined as an inflammatory adipokine.
PARTICIPANTS: Women and men with metabolic syndrome contributed to a cross-sectional study; researchers defined the two sex strata before examining the association.
METHODS: Chemerin was related to a homeostatic insulin resistance index using sex-stratified linear models adjusted for age and waist circumference.
METHODS: Recent infection and systemic steroid treatment were exclusion criteria, and samples from both sexes were mixed within laboratory batches to reduce processing differences.
RESULTS: Among women, each 10 ng/mL higher chemerin corresponded to a significantly higher insulin resistance index (beta 0.21 index units; 95% CI 0.08–0.34; P=.002). The corresponding association was not observed in men.
RESULTS: Median chemerin was 112 [91–138] ng/mL in women and 105 [86–131] ng/mL in men, while the adjusted sex difference in concentration was not significant (P=.13).
DISCUSSION: The positive association was restricted to the female subgroup and should not be interpreted as applying to every participant with metabolic syndrome.
CONCLUSION: The cross-sectional design cannot establish the direction of biological influence, and direct measurements of insulin sensitivity would strengthen subsequent work.
CONCLUSION: These findings support retaining sex-specific estimates when designing larger studies rather than collapsing results into one population-wide coefficient.

article.title: Chemerin and insulin resistance in women attending a prevention clinic
article.abstract:
Insulin resistance varies substantially among women who meet clinical criteria for metabolic syndrome, even when their waist measurements are similar. This investigation assessed the relationship of chemerin to insulin resistance specifically in women with metabolic syndrome. The inflammatory adipokine chemerin was the selected exposure.
A prevention service recruited women with metabolic syndrome for a cross-sectional investigation of their metabolic profile.
Linear regression related the insulin resistance index to chemerin, with the coefficient expressed per 10 ng/mL higher concentration.
The analysis plan specified the homeostatic insulin resistance index as the primary outcome; triglycerides and blood pressure were examined as descriptive secondary measures.
Chemerin showed a positive association with insulin resistance, expressed per 10 ng/mL higher concentration.
Triglycerides also rose across the chemerin distribution (beta 0.07 mmol/L; p = 0.03), whereas the systolic pressure coefficient was close to zero (p = 0.72).
The median age was 51 years [interquartile range 44–59], and no participant had received systemic corticosteroids during the preceding month.
The association was modest in magnitude, and unmeasured inflammatory conditions could still contribute to the pattern observed in this clinic population.
Longitudinal sampling is warranted to establish whether the hormone changes before deterioration in insulin action or merely accompanies the same underlying process.

article.title: Omentin administration and hepatic lipid storage during diet-induced obesity
article.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The relation between circulating omentin and hepatic fat is often studied observationally, leaving uncertainty over its effects in an experimentally controlled metabolic setting. We tested the effect of administered omentin on triglyceride storage in the liver of obese mice.
DESIGN: A laboratory in Spain randomly allocated adult male mice with diet-induced obesity to omentin treatment or vehicle.
METHODS: Omentin was injected daily at 5 micrograms/kg for 4 weeks; an unadjusted two-sample test compared hepatic triglyceride concentration between treatment conditions.
METHODS: Both groups remained on the same high-fat diet, investigators measuring lipid content were masked to allocation, and the terminal assessment followed an overnight fast.
RESULTS: Omentin-treated mice had significantly lower hepatic triglycerides than vehicle-treated mice (p=0.014).
RESULTS: Fasting glucose was also lower by 0.6 mmol/L (p=0.04), but body weight differed by only −0.4 g and the weight comparison was not significant (p=0.62).
RESULTS: All animals assigned to treatment contributed to the liver analysis, and no injection-site reaction requiring treatment was observed.
CONCLUSIONS: The findings are consistent with a small reduction in hepatic lipid storage during short-term omentin exposure under these experimental conditions.
CONCLUSIONS: They do not establish a human treatment effect, and measurement of lipid synthesis and export would help identify the processes responsible for the hepatic response. Interpretation also depends on recognising that a liver concentration represents the balance of several processes: a lower stored pool could arise without any change in food intake, and those pathways cannot be distinguished by this endpoint alone.

article.title: Hepatic triglycerides after sustained omentin exposure in obese mice
article.abstract:
Changes in liver lipid handling following omentin exposure may be small enough to require direct hepatic measurement rather than reliance on circulating glucose alone. The experiment evaluated hepatic triglyceride concentration following repeated omentin administration.
At a separate Spanish laboratory, 32 obese male mice, made obese by diet during adulthood, were randomly assigned: 16 received omentin and 16 received vehicle.
The protocol used daily injections of 5 micrograms/kg for 4 weeks and an unadjusted two-sample test of hepatic triglyceride concentration.
Mice consumed an identical high-fat diet in both groups; masked technicians performed the endpoint measurement after an overnight fast, with no animals excluded from analysis.
Contrary to the prespecified expectation, hepatic triglycerides were significantly higher with omentin than vehicle (mean difference 4.7 mg/g; 95% CI 0.9–8.5).
Glucose differed by 0.1 mmol/L (P = .76), while mean body weight was 0.3 g higher in treated animals (P = .68).
Activity recordings did not suggest a gross treatment-related change, and the animals tolerated the injection schedule without a recorded adverse event.
Under this experimental regimen, increased liver triglyceride storage accompanied omentin administration despite broadly similar body weight and glycaemia.
Because the study measured a terminal lipid pool rather than lipid flux, it cannot distinguish altered synthesis from reduced export; mechanistic follow-up should address that limitation.

article.title: Leptin and central adiposity in adolescents attending community clinics
article.abstract:
AIM: Obesity during adolescence is accompanied by substantial variation in endocrine signals, which may reflect central fat distribution rather than total body size alone. We examined the association between leptin and abdominal size among adolescents living with obesity.
METHODS: A community cross-sectional study assessed adolescents with obesity, aged thirteen to seventeen years; fasting plasma was collected for the hormone assay.
METHODS: Leptin and waist circumference were related in a regression analysis, with the coefficient scaled to a doubling of the hormone.
METHODS: Staff obtained duplicate waist measurements using a common anatomical landmark, and the laboratory team processed samples without access to anthropometric records.
RESULTS: Higher leptin was associated with greater waist circumference per doubling of the hormone.
RESULTS: The median leptin concentration was 24 [16–37] ng/mL, and a secondary model related leptin to higher fasting insulin (beta 1.8 mU/L; p=0.02).
RESULTS: There was no evidence of a leptin association with resting pulse rate in a separate exploratory model (p=0.64).
CONCLUSIONS: The observed waist association supports an endocrine correlate of central adiposity within adolescents already classified as having obesity.
CONCLUSIONS: These cross-sectional data cannot establish temporal ordering, and analyses following pubertal development are needed before the measurement can be interpreted as a predictor of future metabolic change.

article.title: Resistin concentrations and waist measurements in adolescent obesity
article.abstract:
Circulating resistin is influenced by inflammatory activity, yet its relationship with the distribution of body fat in adolescence remains uncertain. The study question was whether resistin concentrations track waist circumference within an adolescent population with obesity.
Norwegian adolescents with obesity contributed hormone measurements and duplicate waist readings to a cross-sectional investigation.
Researchers examined how waist circumference varied across resistin concentrations, presenting the association per doubling of the hormone.
Participants were excluded after a recent febrile illness; waist assessors were unaware of biochemical results, and routine school-based physical activity was recorded by questionnaire.
Resistin was positively associated with waist circumference per doubling of its concentration (beta 1.7 cm; 95% CI 0.4 to 3.0).
An exploratory association with systolic blood pressure was smaller and not significant (beta 0.8 mmHg, P=.28); median resistin was 9.6 [7.2–12.9] ng/mL.
The proportion reporting regular organised sport was similar across resistin thirds, although questionnaire data could not exclude residual differences in activity.
These findings indicate an association between resistin and abdominal size within this adolescent population without implying that resistin directly determines fat distribution.
Repeated measurements spanning growth and changes in pubertal stage may help distinguish persistent metabolic signals from temporary variation associated with adolescent development.

article.title: Oat beta-glucan supplementation and fasting glucose in prediabetes
article.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Viscous cereal fibre can alter nutrient delivery, but its sustained effect on fasting glucose is less certain than its effect during a single meal. We evaluated fasting glycaemia after supplementation with oat beta-glucan in adults with prediabetes. Oat beta-glucan was the soluble cereal fibre used in the intervention.
METHODS: A randomised parallel trial recruited adults with prediabetes to receive oat beta-glucan or a matched cellulose supplement.
INTERVENTION: The primary comparison concerned fasting glucose; a linear model estimated the difference between the two assigned supplements.
METHODS: Both powders were supplied in coded sachets, habitual energy intake was maintained, and unused sachets were counted without revealing allocation to outcome assessors.
RESULTS: Oat beta-glucan produced significantly lower fasting glucose than cellulose.
RESULTS: Postprandial glucose area was also reduced by 7.2% (P=.02), while body weight differed by −0.2 kg between groups (P=.70).
RESULTS: Supplement consumption was reviewed using returned packaging; mild bloating occurred with both products and seldom interrupted the assigned regimen.
CONCLUSIONS: The oat fibre intervention improved fasting glycaemia during this dietary trial without a measurable difference in weight.
CONCLUSIONS: The magnitude is unlikely to replace broader lifestyle measures, and maintenance of the effect beyond the intervention period requires assessment in longer studies with clinically relevant outcomes.

article.title: A blinded cereal fibre trial in adults with raised fasting glucose
article.abstract:
The practical value of adding isolated oat fibre to usual food choices depends on whether sustained metabolic changes occur outside tightly controlled meal tests. Our trial tested whether adding oat beta-glucan improves fasting glucose relative to a cellulose comparator. The tested soluble cereal fibre was oat beta-glucan.
A blinded parallel trial assigned adults with prediabetes to oat beta-glucan or cellulose; the analysis included 84 cellulose recipients.
Daily sachets delivered the assigned supplement, and fasting glucose was the prespecified endpoint.
Participants retained their usual diets and activity patterns, while research staff reviewed adherence diaries before the endpoint assessment.
The trial did not confirm a fasting glucose benefit of oat beta-glucan over cellulose, with no statistically significant difference (mean difference -0.03 mmol/L; 95% CI −0.18–0.12; p=0.69).
Body weight was similarly stable (between-group difference 0.1 kg; p=0.84), although stool frequency increased by 0.5 movements per day with beta-glucan (p=0.01).
Diary completion was high, and gastrointestinal complaints were mild; consumption estimates were comparable between the two coded products.
An explicit absence of a detectable glycaemic benefit in this trial should not be interpreted as proof that every formulation or dose is ineffective.
Nevertheless, these results do not support promising a reduction in fasting glucose when this amount of isolated fibre is added to the habitual diet over the tested interval.

article.title: Walnut replacement and circulating triglycerides in metabolic syndrome
article.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Replacing an energy-dense snack with nuts could improve metabolic risk, although changes in individual lipid fractions may not move together. We sought to quantify the triglyceride response when walnuts replace a usual snack. Walnuts represented a tree nut substitution rather than an added supplement.
METHODS: A crossover trial recruited adults with metabolic syndrome to walnut and energy-matched cracker periods, with the sequence set by random allocation.
METHODS: Each dietary period lasted 6 weeks, separated by a washout; mixed models of fasting serum triglycerides included treatment, period and baseline triglycerides.
METHODS: Participants were asked to substitute the provided food for an existing snack, not add it to usual intake, and dietary records were reviewed at the end of each period.
RESULTS: Triglycerides were lower after walnuts than after crackers (adjusted mean difference -0.16 mmol/L; 95% CI −0.28 to −0.04).
RESULTS: The paired difference in body weight was 0.1 kg (p=0.77), and fasting glucose differed by −0.04 mmol/L (p=0.58).
RESULTS: Adherence estimated from returned packets averaged 91%, and no participant withdrew because of a reported allergic reaction.
CONCLUSION: The observed triglyceride reduction supports food substitution as a potentially useful component of dietary management in metabolic syndrome.
CONCLUSION: Because this short study does not address cardiovascular events, any clinical interpretation should remain limited to the measured biochemical response and to people able to tolerate nuts.

article.title: Blood pressure during walnut and cracker snack periods
article.abstract:
Dietary recommendations for metabolic syndrome usually combine several goals, making it useful to identify which outcome responds to a specific food substitution. The aim was to measure systolic pressure during walnut and cracker snack periods. The tree nut intervention consisted of walnuts.
In a Portuguese crossover experiment, adults with metabolic syndrome received walnuts and energy-matched crackers in random order.
A mixed model compared seated systolic blood pressure between the walnut and cracker conditions.
A washout separated the interventions, and trained staff calculated resting pressure as the average of three automated readings.
Walnuts yielded significantly lower systolic pressure than crackers.
The diastolic difference was −0.8 mmHg (P = .31), and mean body weight remained similar between dietary periods (difference −0.1 kg; P = .88).
Diet records suggested that participants generally replaced their usual snack rather than increasing total energy consumption, although self-report could not exclude small changes.
The systolic response was modest and should be interpreted alongside existing antihypertensive management, which was kept stable during participation.
Larger pragmatic studies would be useful to determine whether this food substitution can be maintained over longer intervals and whether comparable effects appear outside a closely supported research setting.

article.title: A Mediterranean dietary programme and liver fat in steatotic liver disease
article.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nutrition is central to managing metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, yet changes during a programme do not necessarily isolate the effect of its dietary pattern. This trial estimated the liver fat response to Mediterranean dietary counselling compared with usual advice. The intervention targeted a dietary pattern rather than one nutrient.
METHODS: A randomised outpatient trial recruited adults with steatotic liver disease to Mediterranean dietary counselling or usual dietary advice.
METHODS: Liver fat measured by magnetic resonance imaging was compared between the assigned dietary counselling groups.
INTERVENTION: The programme emphasised vegetables, legumes, whole grains, olive oil and fish; both arms received the same recommendation for moderate physical activity without a prescribed calorie target.
RESULTS: Liver fat was lower with Mediterranean dietary counselling than with usual advice.
RESULTS: Alanine aminotransferase differed by −5.8 U/L (p=0.03), while the between-group weight difference was −1.1 kg (p=0.08).
RESULTS: Attendance at counselling sessions exceeded 80%, and reported physical activity changed similarly in the two arms during follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS: Structured advice on a Mediterranean eating pattern produced a modest incremental reduction in liver fat relative to the study comparator.
CONCLUSIONS: The findings apply to the tested outpatient programme; they do not identify the separate contributions of individual foods or establish an effect on long-term liver complications.

article.title: Liver fat before and after a community Mediterranean diet course
article.abstract:
Community dietary courses are easier to deliver than controlled feeding, but their evaluation requires careful distinction between change over time and a treatment contrast. We assessed how liver fat changed over the course of a community Mediterranean diet programme. Mediterranean eating was treated as a dietary pattern.
An uncontrolled prospective programme in Croatia recruited adults with steatotic liver disease for a community Mediterranean diet course.
Liver fat percentage was measured by magnetic resonance imaging at entry and after 20 weeks; a paired test evaluated change among participants completing both scans.
Weekly group sessions encouraged vegetables, pulses, olive oil and fish while discussing shopping and meal preparation; there was no separate reference group or random allocation.
At follow-up, liver fat was lower than at entry.
Body weight decreased by 2.0 kg (P=.004), and alanine aminotransferase decreased by 6.3 U/L (P=.02); the study did not attempt to separate these correlated changes.
Participants completing imaging attended most of the scheduled sessions, and those unable to attend were offered written summaries of the practical advice.
The observed improvement shows that the programme coincided with lower liver fat among completers, but regression to the mean and concurrent behaviour changes remain possible explanations.
A controlled evaluation would be necessary to estimate how much of the change is attributable specifically to the dietary pattern rather than to participation in the programme.

article.title: Early time-restricted eating and fasting glucose in adults with prediabetes
article.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Limiting daily eating to an earlier interval may influence fasting glucose without requiring a prescribed energy deficit, but responses may depend on the population studied. We tested an early eating window for its effect on fasting glucose in adults with prediabetes.
DESIGN: A randomised trial analysed 108 adults with prediabetes, assigning 54 to an early eating window and 54 to their usual eating schedule.
METHODS: The intervention allowed food between 08:00 and 16:00 for 8 weeks; fasting glucose was the primary metabolic endpoint.
METHODS: Participants received advice to maintain habitual energy intake, and the control group recorded meal timing with the same application to balance monitoring demands.
RESULTS: The early-window group had significantly lower fasting glucose than the usual-schedule group (mean difference -0.22 mmol/L; p=0.012).
RESULTS: Weight differed by −0.7 kg between groups (p=0.15), while the daily eating interval shortened by 3.6 hours in the intervention arm relative to control (p<0.001).
RESULTS: No severe hypoglycaemic episode was reported, and participants completed food records on a median of 49 days during the intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: Earlier meal timing modestly improved fasting glucose in adults already showing dysglycaemia under this short, monitored regimen.
CONCLUSIONS: The result should not be assumed to apply across developmental stages; research in younger populations requires direct measurement of glycaemic responses and attention to feasibility during school days.

article.title: An early eating window during adolescence: a randomised feasibility trial
article.abstract:
Meal-timing interventions designed for adults may interact differently with growth, school routines and the metabolic physiology of adolescence. Our primary question concerned the fasting glucose response to an early eating schedule in adolescents with obesity.
Adolescents with obesity entered a randomised trial of early time-restricted eating compared with their usual meal schedule.
Food was permitted from 08:00 until 16:00 for 8 weeks, and the primary endpoint was fasting glucose measured at the final assessment.
Families were asked to preserve total energy intake, both groups logged meals electronically, and dietitians reviewed records to identify persistent difficulty following the assigned schedule.
Fasting glucose was significantly higher in the early-window arm than with the usual schedule.
The eating interval shortened by 3.4 hours (P<.001), whereas the body-weight contrast was −0.2 kg and not significant (P=.74).
The glucose values remained within the laboratory reference range for most participants, and no serious intervention-related event was recorded during follow-up.
This adolescent trial therefore did not reproduce the expected favourable direction of the fasting glucose response, despite a measurable change in meal timing.
Developmental stage and the absence of established prediabetes are relevant features of this population; adult recommendations should not be transferred to adolescents without further direct evidence.

article.title: Glycated haemoglobin following metformin initiation in outpatient diabetes care
article.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early treatment decisions in diabetes often rely on the expected biochemical response before evidence about persistence is available. We assessed the change in glycated haemoglobin after metformin initiation in previously untreated diabetes. Metformin was the glucose-lowering medication under evaluation.
METHODS: A prospective treatment cohort recruited adults with newly diagnosed diabetes who had not previously used glucose-lowering medication.
METHODS: Glycated haemoglobin was compared with the pretreatment measurement using a paired analysis of patients with measurements at both visits.
PROCEDURES: Participants attended a shared education session about food choices, and clinicians reviewed tolerability before deciding whether to continue treatment.
RESULTS: Glycated haemoglobin declined after metformin initiation relative to the pretreatment value.
RESULTS: Fasting glucose also moved downward, whereas weight showed considerable variation between individuals despite generally stable activity records.
RESULTS: Digestive complaints were concentrated near treatment initiation; clinical records contained no episode of severe hypoglycaemia.
CONCLUSIONS: The biochemical pattern supports a favourable early response to starting metformin in this selected outpatient population.
CONCLUSIONS: Because there was no untreated comparison group, regression to the mean and concurrent changes in behaviour could contribute to the findings. Follow-up beyond the initial assessment is needed to establish persistence, and future evaluations should document the reasons for treatment discontinuation rather than relying only on measurements from people who remain in care.

article.title: Early glycaemic changes among people beginning metformin therapy
article.abstract:
For people beginning diabetes treatment, the expected biochemical response to medication is an important part of shared management planning. This prospective study evaluated change in glycated haemoglobin after metformin was introduced in outpatient care. The glucose-lowering medication studied here was metformin.
At outpatient centres, adults with newly diagnosed diabetes and no previous glucose-lowering drug use began metformin and returned for reassessment.
Whole-blood glycated haemoglobin was measured before treatment and again during therapy, with the analysis comparing observations from the same person.
Education addressed food choices and activity alongside medication; clinicians reviewed persistent symptoms and could revise management when necessary.
Glycated haemoglobin was lower during metformin treatment than before initiation.
Fasting glucose followed a similar direction, while weight records showed little consistent movement across the cohort.
Gastrointestinal symptoms were generally short-lived, and no severe hypoglycaemic event was recorded in the available clinical notes.
The observed glycaemic reduction is consistent with an early response when metformin is introduced in previously untreated diabetes.
This observational comparison does not isolate medication from changes made at diagnosis, and incomplete follow-up could favour people finding treatment easier to continue. A subsequent evaluation should include those who stop therapy, describe the reasons for doing so and determine whether initial improvement persists as everyday treatment routines become established.

article.title: Albumin excretion before and after empagliflozin initiation
article.abstract:
AIMS: Changes in urinary albumin may precede major loss of filtration, but an early biochemical response need not indicate long-term renal protection. We examined albumin excretion before and after empagliflozin initiation in adults with mild albuminuria. Empagliflozin was evaluated as a renal glucose transport inhibitor.
METHODS: An Austrian prospective treatment study recruited adults with diabetes and mild albuminuria when clinicians prescribed empagliflozin.
METHODS: Investigators compared the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio with its pretreatment value using a paired log-scale model.
PROCEDURES: Background renin–angiotensin system therapy remained stable, and staff checked collection records before calculating the endpoint.
RESULTS: The urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio was reduced after empagliflozin initiation relative to baseline.
RESULTS: Systolic pressure also declined, whereas filtration-rate estimates varied between visits without a clear common direction.
RESULTS: There was no treatment cessation attributed to symptomatic volume depletion in the follow-up records reviewed for this study.
CONCLUSIONS: A lower albumin ratio accompanied empagliflozin initiation in the selected clinical population.
CONCLUSIONS: Without a concurrent untreated group, the contribution of repeated measurement and changes in everyday management remains uncertain. The study therefore cannot establish whether the observed biochemical response predicts later preservation of kidney function. Continued observation should assess sustained response and clinically meaningful outcomes, including participants whose medication is subsequently changed rather than restricting follow-up to persistent users.

article.title: An outpatient cohort examining albuminuria during empagliflozin treatment
article.abstract:
Urinary albumin varies between visits, so an average response to newly started therapy may not be consistently demonstrated in small clinical cohorts. We asked whether the albumin ratio falls after empagliflozin is introduced under stable background treatment. The renal glucose transport inhibitor empagliflozin was prescribed as part of usual care.
A prospective outpatient cohort recruited adults with diabetes and mild albuminuria at the start of empagliflozin therapy.
The primary analysis compared the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio during treatment with its pretreatment value; no separate control cohort was enrolled.
Background renin–angiotensin system treatment remained unchanged, and the laboratory received coded records without information about visit order.
The study did not confirm a reduction in albumin-to-creatinine ratio after empagliflozin initiation relative to baseline.
Systolic blood pressure declined during observation, whereas filtration measurements fluctuated without a consistent pattern across individuals.
No withdrawal was attributed to symptomatic low blood pressure, although routine clinical records could not capture every transient complaint.
The albuminuria finding offers no confirmation of an early biochemical response in this cohort despite the accompanying blood-pressure change.
Visit-to-visit variation and selective return for assessment remain plausible influences on the result. Further evaluation should standardise collection conditions, retain people who discontinue therapy in follow-up and avoid treating an inconclusive biochemical comparison as evidence about the prevention of future clinical kidney events.

article.title: Adiponectin change after pioglitazone initiation in insulin resistance
article.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Insulin-sensitising therapy can change adipose-derived hormones, but the magnitude of the circulating response varies with baseline metabolic status. We assessed change in adiponectin after pioglitazone initiation in people with insulin resistance. The intervention used the insulin sensitiser pioglitazone.
METHODS: Adults with insulin resistance and central obesity joined a prospective cohort when their clinicians introduced pioglitazone.
METHODS: Adiponectin was the primary endpoint, with linear regression used to summarise within-person change from the pretreatment measurement.
METHODS: Participants were advised to continue their usual diet and activity, and clinical reviews included checks for oedema and other symptoms that might require discontinuation.
RESULTS: Adiponectin increased relative to baseline during pioglitazone treatment, and the change was statistically significant (p=0.004).
RESULTS: Fasting insulin declined by 2.2 mU/L (p=0.03), whereas body weight rose by 0.8 kg (p=0.04) relative to the pretreatment values.
RESULTS: Ankle swelling was monitored at visits, and participants were advised to report persistent symptoms between appointments.
CONCLUSIONS: The hormone response was compatible with altered adipose signalling during pioglitazone exposure, alongside small changes in insulin and body weight.
CONCLUSIONS: These biochemical observations do not justify treatment on their own, especially without a concurrent untreated cohort. Subsequent studies seeking clinical benefit must weigh adverse effects and patient selection rather than interpreting a biomarker increase as a sufficient therapeutic endpoint.

article.title: An outpatient cohort examining early adiponectin response to pioglitazone
article.abstract:
Whether a brief course of insulin-sensitising therapy produces a reliably detectable adiponectin response is relevant to the design of mechanistic studies. Our purpose was to estimate change in adiponectin during a brief exposure to pioglitazone. Pioglitazone belongs to the insulin sensitiser class.
At a Slovak outpatient service, adults with central obesity and insulin resistance entered a prospective cohort at pioglitazone initiation.
Pioglitazone was administered at 15 mg/day for 6 weeks; a linear model estimated within-person adiponectin change with the baseline concentration included as a covariate.
Diet and physical activity advice accompanied the medication, while clinicians assessed ankle swelling and other possible tolerability problems during follow-up.
The estimated change from baseline indicated higher adiponectin during pioglitazone treatment but was not statistically significant (mean change 0.7 micrograms/mL; 95% CI −0.2 to 1.6; P=.12).
Fasting insulin decreased by 1.1 mU/L (P=.18), and weight increased by 0.4 kg (P=.21), with intervals too wide to support precise estimates of these secondary changes.
Some participants reported mild ankle swelling; the adiponectin measurements remained available despite these symptoms.
The adiponectin estimate points upward but remains uncertain in this short study, so neither a clearly established increase nor an absence of biological response can be claimed.
A larger design with repeated hormone measurements and a concurrent comparison cohort would help separate sampling variability from the physiological response and from changes that accompany starting treatment.

article.title: Lipid change during acarbose use in metabolic syndrome
article.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Delayed carbohydrate absorption may influence lipid metabolism as well as postprandial glucose, although small lipid changes require careful measurement. We investigated change in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol after acarbose initiation in metabolic syndrome with prediabetes. Acarbose was studied as a carbohydrate absorption inhibitor.
METHODS: A prospective treatment cohort in Germany recruited adults with metabolic syndrome and prediabetes who were beginning acarbose.
METHODS: The regimen provided 50 mg with each main meal for 12 weeks; a linear model estimated within-person cholesterol change with the baseline concentration included for adjustment.
PROCEDURES: Lipid-lowering medication remained unchanged, dietary guidance was maintained throughout observation, and a masked laboratory used an enzymatic assay for the endpoint.
RESULTS: Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol declined from baseline during acarbose treatment.
RESULTS: Post-meal glucose decreased by 0.7 mmol/L relative to pretreatment (p=0.008), while body weight changed by −0.3 kg (p=0.48).
RESULTS: Mild flatulence was reported during acarbose use, but no participant required hospital care or discontinued follow-up because of gastrointestinal symptoms.
CONCLUSIONS: A small favourable lipid change accompanied the expected postprandial glucose response in this population under the tested regimen.
CONCLUSIONS: The result needs confirmation because the cohort was observed briefly and had no untreated reference population. Cardiovascular outcomes were not measured, so the biochemical pattern should not be treated as evidence that acarbose replaces established lipid-lowering therapy.

article.title: Cholesterol trajectories following acarbose initiation in a separate cohort
article.abstract:
Glucose-lowering interventions do not necessarily move every cardiovascular risk marker in a favourable direction, making separate lipid assessment worthwhile. We evaluated within-person changes in fasting low-density lipoprotein cholesterol after starting acarbose. The carbohydrate absorption inhibitor selected for testing was acarbose.
An independent prospective cohort in Germany enrolled adults beginning acarbose who had metabolic syndrome accompanied by prediabetes.
The acarbose dose was 50 mg at every main meal during a 12-week regimen; linear regression described change from baseline cholesterol, retaining the initial concentration as a covariate.
Dietary advice was kept constant, lipid-lowering medication was not modified, and masked technicians used an enzymatic assay.
Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol was higher than at baseline during acarbose therapy (adjusted mean change 0.12 mmol/L; 95% CI 0.02–0.22).
In contrast, post-meal glucose decreased by 0.6 mmol/L (P=.01), while the weight change was −0.2 kg and not significant (P=.63).
Gastrointestinal symptoms were generally mild and did not lead to hospital admission or loss of endpoint measurements.
The small increase in the lipid endpoint occurred alongside improved post-meal glycaemia, illustrating that these biochemical responses can diverge during follow-up.
Because neither lipoprotein turnover nor cardiovascular events were measured, the mechanism and clinical implications of the lipid finding remain unresolved. A concurrent untreated cohort would also help distinguish medication-related change from influences accompanying routine management.

article.title: Irisin and insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in cultured human myotubes
article.abstract: Whether circulating irisin can directly modify skeletal muscle glucose handling remains uncertain, because circulating concentrations may reflect several tissues rather than muscle activity alone. Irisin is a muscle-derived signalling protein with proposed effects on substrate handling. We examined the change in insulin-stimulated glucose uptake after recombinant irisin exposure in primary human myotubes, using donor cultures as the independent experimental units. A laboratory experiment in Denmark used cultures from 18 adult donors with obesity; glucose transport was measured before exposure and again after 24 hours of incubation with irisin supplied at 10 ng/mL. Fluorescent uptake after a fixed insulin challenge was compared with each donor culture at baseline using a paired test; viability and lactate release were secondary measurements. Only donor cultures yielding paired uptake measurements entered the primary comparison. Glucose uptake was higher after irisin exposure than at baseline (mean change from baseline 11.6 percentage points; 95% CI 4.2 to 19.0); this finding was statistically significant. Cell viability remained above 94%, whereas lactate release rose by 6% after incubation without meeting the statistical threshold for that secondary measurement (P = .19). The uptake response was present in cultures from both women and men, although the experiment was not powered to compare the sexes or investigate differences related to medication history. These observations support a direct action of irisin on glucose transport under the conditions tested; they do not establish that the concentrations achieved in patients reproduce this cellular response.

article.title: Glucose transport after short irisin exposure in donor-derived muscle cells
article.abstract: Muscle cells retain metabolic features of their donors after differentiation, providing a practical system for testing whether irisin alters their acute response to insulin. As a muscle-derived signalling protein, irisin offers a means of probing transport regulation. A Swedish laboratory experiment followed donor-derived primary human myotubes from adults with obesity before and after exposure to irisin. Cultures were incubated for 24 hours with 10 ng/mL irisin, then challenged with insulin before fluorescent glucose uptake was quantified in washed cells. Our objective was to establish whether uptake changed from its pretreatment value; a paired test compared donor averages, with glycogen content and viability as secondary outcomes. Both pretreatment and post-incubation readings were required for a culture to contribute. Uptake increased after irisin incubation compared with the pretreatment measurement (p=0.012); this finding was statistically significant. Glycogen content increased by 7.1% from baseline, while viability changed by only 0.4 percentage points and remained within the laboratory acceptance range in every donor culture. The response indicates enhanced transport in this cell system rather than evidence of improved whole-body insulin sensitivity; tissue exposure, clearance and counter-regulatory responses cannot be reconstructed in these dishes. Further work should establish whether the uptake change persists after the recombinant protein is removed and whether it varies with the metabolic state of the donor.

article.title: Fetuin-A and fasting insulin resistance in adults with fatty liver
article.abstract: Fetuin-A links hepatic secretion to peripheral metabolism, but its relationship with insulin resistance may depend on the stage of metabolic disease rather than a universal circulating threshold. The liver-derived protein fetuin-A may connect hepatic function with peripheral glucose handling. Our cross-sectional study tested the association between fetuin-A and fasting insulin resistance, assessed using the homeostasis model, in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. Adult outpatients with this liver condition underwent a metabolic assessment before receiving their laboratory results, allowing the clinical evaluation to be recorded independently of the protein measurement. Insulin resistance was related to fetuin-A concentrations; waist circumference and alanine aminotransferase provided additional descriptions of the metabolic phenotype. Higher fetuin-A was associated with a higher insulin resistance index. Waist circumference tended to increase across the concentration range, whereas alanine aminotransferase showed no clear linear relationship; neither secondary observation established a direction of causation. The observed gradient is compatible with a relation between hepatic metabolic dysfunction and insulin resistance, although the simultaneous measurements cannot establish which process comes first. Because recruitment required established fatty liver, these data should not be extrapolated to otherwise healthy young people whose hepatic fat content and hormonal environment may differ.

article.title: Fetuin-A concentrations and insulin sensitivity during adolescence
article.abstract: We investigated whether fetuin-A was associated with fasting insulin resistance in adolescents without liver disease, a population in which pubertal changes complicate the interpretation of metabolic markers. Fetuin-A, a liver-derived protein, could behave differently during pubertal maturation. This cross-sectional survey in Portugal recruited adolescents attending school health assessments, all without diabetes or evidence of fatty liver. Fetuin-A was assessed alongside an insulin resistance index obtained from the homeostasis model; clinical records and a routine examination established eligibility independently of the laboratory measurements. An age- and sex-adjusted linear regression estimated the association per 100 microgram/mL higher fetuin-A, with waist circumference and fasting triglycerides examined as secondary outcomes. Adolescents contributed when both primary measurements were available. Fetuin-A was inversely associated with the insulin resistance index (adjusted beta -0.27 index units per 100 microgram/mL; 95% CI -0.45 to -0.09). The association with waist circumference was weak, while triglycerides were lower at higher fetuin-A concentrations; these secondary observations did not establish a biological pathway. An inverse relationship in adolescents does not imply that raising fetuin-A would improve metabolism; maturation and the absence of liver disease distinguish this setting from clinical samples of older patients. Longitudinal measurements through puberty would help determine whether the association reflects transient developmental physiology or predicts a persistent difference in insulin handling later in life.

article.title: Visfatin and fasting glucose in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
article.abstract: Adipose-derived proteins have been proposed as markers of dysglycaemia in polycystic ovary syndrome, but individual proteins may represent different inflammatory and metabolic pathways. Visfatin is an adipose-associated protein that may accompany disturbed glucose regulation. We evaluated whether visfatin concentration tracked fasting glucose among women with polycystic ovary syndrome who had not started glucose-lowering treatment. Women with untreated polycystic ovary syndrome were recruited through endocrine clinics, with fasting glucose and visfatin determined from the same assessment. The relation between visfatin and glucose was examined across the observed concentration range; insulin and waist circumference were additional metabolic measurements. Higher visfatin was associated with higher fasting glucose (P = 0.004); this finding was statistically significant. The association with insulin was stronger than that with waist circumference, suggesting that the measured features did not all track visfatin in the same way. Median visfatin was 13.4 ng/mL [interquartile range 9.6–18.2], and repeating the glucose assay in stored aliquots produced a mean difference below 1 mg/dL. The findings identify an association within this selected clinical population; neither the temporal order of the changes nor the clinical value of adding visfatin to routine testing was established. Clinical records were checked before laboratory analyses, and none of the women had begun treatment intended to improve glucose regulation at enrolment.

article.title: Apelin as a correlate of fasting glycaemia in untreated ovarian syndrome
article.abstract: Apelin signalling has metabolic actions distinct from those of several other adipokines, prompting an examination of its association with fasting glucose in polycystic ovary syndrome. The signalling peptide apelin provides a candidate link between adipose biology and glycaemia. An observational investigation recruited untreated women with polycystic ovary syndrome through specialist outpatient services to examine apelin alongside fasting glucose. Glucose-lowering medication was an exclusion criterion; laboratory staff were unaware of clinical measurements, and the report did not designate a restricted subgroup for the primary association. Linear regression estimated the glucose association per 100 pg/mL higher apelin; insulin and blood pressure were explored as secondary outcomes. Apelin was inversely associated with fasting glucose. The apelin–insulin association was weak, while systolic pressure was 1.6 mmHg lower per increment; neither secondary association reached the study threshold for statistical significance. Median apelin was 462 pg/mL, and laboratory quality checks identified no systematic relation between assay variability and fasting glucose across the observed concentration range. Apelin may mark a component of glucose regulation in untreated women, but these cross-sectional observations do not establish a therapeutic effect or justify using apelin concentrations as a diagnostic threshold.

article.title: Retinol-binding protein in adults with and without metabolic syndrome
article.abstract: Retinol-binding protein may reflect altered hepatic and adipose signalling, but its association with established metabolic syndrome is difficult to separate from the characteristics of the people recruited. This retinol transport protein also participates in signalling beyond vitamin transport. This case-control study examined whether higher retinol-binding protein was associated with the presence of metabolic syndrome in adults attending community health services. The case-control analysis compared adults meeting the clinical criteria for metabolic syndrome with community controls who did not meet those criteria; clinical status was established before protein measurements were disclosed. Logistic regression estimated the odds of metabolic syndrome per 10 mg/L greater retinol-binding protein, with age and sex included as covariates; waist circumference and fasting glucose were secondary descriptive measurements. The main analysis used cases and controls with a measured protein concentration. Higher retinol-binding protein was associated with greater odds of metabolic syndrome (adjusted odds ratio 1.31; 95% CI 1.10 to 1.56; p = 0.003); this finding was statistically significant. Median protein concentration was 48 mg/L among cases and 40 mg/L among controls; waist circumference differed by 12.6 cm, whereas fasting glucose differed by 14.8 mg/dL between the two groups. Excluding adults who reported recent acute illness produced a similar direction of association, although fewer participants remained available for that sensitivity analysis. The association identifies a circulating correlate of existing metabolic syndrome rather than a predictor of future disease; selection of controls and residual confounding remain important limitations of this comparison.

article.title: Retinol-binding protein in a community case-control comparison
article.abstract: We investigated the relationship of retinol-binding protein to prevalent metabolic syndrome using cases and controls drawn from the same community screening service. Retinol-binding protein belongs to the retinol transport protein family, but its metabolic associations remain unsettled. A case-control investigation compared adults with metabolic syndrome and controls without the syndrome, recruited through the same screening service. Clinical classifications were recorded independently of laboratory results; fasting glucose and waist circumference characterised the metabolic differences between the comparison groups. The primary analysis related retinol-binding protein to the presence of metabolic syndrome, while the clinical measurements provided a broader description of the recruited groups. Greater retinol-binding protein concentrations accompanied higher odds of metabolic syndrome; this finding was statistically significant. Cases had a median protein concentration of 46 mg/L, compared with 39 mg/L in controls; the median waist difference was 11.3 cm, and fasting glucose was 13.2 mg/dL higher among cases. Removing participants who had recently changed lipid-lowering treatment did not change the direction of the association, but fewer observations remained available. The findings support an association with existing metabolic abnormalities, while the case-control design cannot determine whether changes in the protein preceded the syndrome or resulted from its metabolic consequences. The syndrome definition required several metabolic abnormalities, so no individual component should be interpreted as equivalent to the composite clinical classification.

article.title: Replacing refined starch with lentils and fasting triglycerides in prediabetes
article.abstract: Pulse foods can replace rapidly digested starch without requiring a broadly restrictive diet, but effects on fasting lipids may depend on the foods actually displaced. Lentils provide a pulse food that can be incorporated into familiar meals. This randomized trial assessed whether a daily lentil portion replacing refined rice lowered fasting triglycerides in adults with prediabetes. Participants received either cooked lentils or refined rice in energy-matched meals; instructions addressed preparation and portion consistency without prescribing a wider dietary restriction. Fasting triglycerides were compared between the assigned diets; body weight and fasting glucose were prespecified secondary outcomes. The lentil group had lower fasting triglycerides than the rice group; this finding was statistically significant. Body weight differed by -0.6 kg between groups, and fasting glucose was 3.1 mg/dL lower with lentils; the latter difference remained within a clinically modest range. Recorded meal adherence exceeded 86% in each arm, while transient bloating was reported by nine lentil recipients and four rice recipients without requiring withdrawal. A simple substitution of lentils for refined rice improved fasting triglycerides in this trial; the result should be interpreted as an effect of the substitution and does not isolate a single nutrient mechanism. Meal preparation instructions were designed to be practical in ordinary households, while the supplied portions helped distinguish the food substitution from general dietary advice.

article.title: Lentil-based lunches and the lipid profile of adults with impaired glycaemia
article.abstract: We tested a practical lunch substitution in adults with prediabetes to determine whether replacing refined rice with cooked lentils changed fasting triglycerides. Replacing rice with a pulse food such as lentils changes several dietary components simultaneously. A randomized feeding trial in Australia retained 79 adults assigned to lentil lunches; the comparison group received refined rice lunches. Accompanying foods were selected to keep energy intake similar between the two diets, and participants recorded whether they consumed or discarded each supplied lunch. Regression compared triglycerides with adjustment for their baseline value; secondary outcomes comprised waist circumference and fasting glucose, while meal records assessed adherence. Attendance at the triglyceride assessment defined the analysed population. The trial did not confirm a triglyceride-lowering effect of lentils relative to rice (adjusted mean difference -1.4 mg/dL; 95% CI -9.8 to 7.0; p=0.74); this finding was not statistically significant. Waist circumference was 0.5 cm lower in the lentil group, and fasting glucose differed by -1.0 mg/dL; confidence intervals for both secondary estimates included zero. Participants consumed a median of 91% of supplied lunches, with similar adherence across groups; gastrointestinal complaints were mild and did not account for missed outcome visits. Lentil substitution was feasible but did not produce a detectable triglyceride benefit under these conditions; uncertainty remains compatible with a modest reduction and should not be interpreted as proof of exact equivalence.

article.title: Extra virgin olive oil substitution and triglycerides in metabolic syndrome
article.abstract: We evaluated fasting triglyceride change when adults with metabolic syndrome replaced their habitual refined sunflower oil with extra virgin olive oil, a plant oil used in ordinary cooking. A prospective dietary intervention at an urban outpatient clinic in Spain followed participants before and after this oil substitution, without prescribing other changes to their usual diet. Participants used 25 mL daily for eight weeks; triglycerides were measured before the exchange and at completion under one laboratory protocol, following an overnight fast. A linear model evaluated the within-person change from baseline, with body weight and fasting glucose as secondary measurements; adults with both triglyceride measurements formed the analysis set. Fasting triglycerides declined during olive-oil substitution (mean change from baseline -7.8 mg/dL). Mean body weight changed by -0.1 kg and fasting glucose by -0.7 mg/dL; neither secondary finding indicated a substantial metabolic change during the intervention. Returned containers suggested consistent use of the supplied oil, and no participant altered lipid-lowering medication; the investigators also checked whether additional dietary supplements had been introduced. The replacement accompanied a small triglyceride reduction in this setting, although the clinical importance and persistence of the change remain uncertain; without an untreated comparison, the observed course cannot be attributed exclusively to the oil exchange.

article.title: Fasting lipids during an olive oil exchange intervention
article.abstract: Small changes in dietary fat sources may influence circulating triglycerides even when weight remains stable, motivating an investigation of extra virgin olive oil as a plant oil intervention. We examined change from pretreatment triglycerides after adults with metabolic syndrome attending an urban Spanish outpatient clinic exchanged refined sunflower oil for olive oil in a prospective dietary intervention. The prescribed olive-oil quantity was 25 mL daily, supplied for eight weeks while participants maintained the rest of their usual diet; fasting measurements preceded and followed the substitution. Within-person triglyceride changes were evaluated by a linear model, retaining adults who supplied both baseline and endpoint measurements; weight and fasting glycaemia provided additional metabolic observations. Triglyceride concentrations increased during the olive-oil intervention relative to the pretreatment values recorded while participants were using sunflower oil. Weight changed little, with a mean increase of 0.2 kg; fasting glucose rose by 0.6 mg/dL, but its uncertainty interval included no change. Medication regimens remained stable, container returns supported adherence to the oil prescription, and participants reported no new dietary supplements during follow-up. The positive triglyceride change was unexpected and requires confirmation; the lack of an untreated group prevents attribution to a particular mechanism, but the observations do not support a lipid benefit from this substitution under the conditions studied.

article.title: Ground flaxseed and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in postmenopausal women
article.abstract: Ground flaxseed provides fibre and unsaturated fat, and its effects on lipids may be relevant to postmenopausal women whose metabolic risk is increasing. Flaxseed is a fibre-rich seed with several components that could influence metabolism. We examined whether adding ground flaxseed to breakfast changed fasting low-density lipoprotein cholesterol from its pretreatment value in postmenopausal women with central obesity. A prospective dietary intervention asked participants to incorporate ground flaxseed into their usual breakfast without replacing other meals or starting a structured weight-loss programme. A paired comparison evaluated the cholesterol change from baseline; fasting triglycerides and waist circumference were secondary outcomes. The paired analysis retained women with both cholesterol measurements. Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol decreased from baseline during flaxseed supplementation. Triglycerides fell by 4.3 mg/dL and waist circumference by 0.8 cm, with uncertainty intervals including zero for both secondary changes. Supplement records suggested median adherence of 88%, and mild gastrointestinal symptoms were recorded without prompting anyone to stop the supplement. The observed cholesterol reduction accompanied flaxseed supplementation, although other aspects of cardiovascular risk were not evaluated and the findings cannot establish a reduction in clinical events. The absence of an untreated group limits attribution of the observed change, because seasonal eating habits and other unrecorded behaviours may have changed concurrently.

article.title: Glycated haemoglobin after flaxseed supplementation in central obesity
article.abstract: This study addressed whether a breakfast supplement of ground flaxseed changes glycated haemoglobin from baseline in postmenopausal women with central obesity, rather than testing its lipid effects. This fibre-rich seed offers a practical addition to meals without requiring a comprehensive dietary programme. A prospective intervention provided ground flaxseed for breakfast to postmenopausal women with central obesity, with no comparison supplement or prescribed weight-loss programme. Glycated haemoglobin was measured before supplementation and at completion; waist circumference and fasting glucose were recorded to describe accompanying metabolic changes. A paired test evaluated the change in glycated haemoglobin from baseline; adherence was described separately rather than used to exclude women from this comparison. Glycated haemoglobin decreased from its baseline value with flaxseed. Fasting glucose fell by 2.6 mg/dL, whereas waist circumference changed by -0.4 cm; the latter change was not distinguishable from zero at the study threshold. Median adherence was 90%, and no serious supplement-related event occurred; women reporting bloating generally continued the supplement after dividing it between two meals. The observed glycaemic difference was small, and its durability is unknown; these findings should not be interpreted as evidence about cholesterol because that outcome was not measured in this investigation. Participants received instructions for incorporating the seed into familiar foods, and the investigators distinguished gastrointestinal discomfort from symptoms requiring medical assessment.

article.title: Vitamin D and fasting insulin in adults with low vitamin status
article.abstract: Low vitamin D status often accompanies obesity, but supplementation studies must separate the effects of vitamin replacement from other components of metabolic care. We tested whether vitamin D supplementation reduced fasting insulin compared with placebo in adults with obesity and low circulating vitamin D concentrations. A double-blind randomized trial enrolled adults with low vitamin D status and obesity, allocating vitamin D or matching placebo at an active dose of 2000 IU daily. Insulin was measured after an overnight fast; linear regression compared final values after adjustment for baseline insulin, with calcium and fasting glucose as secondary measurements. The evaluated population comprised participants with a final fasting insulin result. Fasting insulin was lower with vitamin D than placebo (adjusted mean difference -1.8 mIU/L; 95% CI -3.2 to -0.4); this finding was statistically significant. Calcium remained within the laboratory reference range in both groups, while fasting glucose differed by -1.9 mg/dL and its confidence interval included zero. Vitamin status improved in the active group, with a median circulating concentration increase of 18 ng/mL, but body weight was stable and no participant started a new glucose-lowering medicine. Vitamin replacement produced a modest insulin difference in deficient adults with obesity; the result does not establish benefit in people with adequate vitamin status or support replacement of established metabolic treatments.

article.title: Vitamin replacement and fasting insulin during a winter intervention
article.abstract: Winter vitamin D replacement was investigated as a possible modifier of fasting insulin in adults with obesity whose screening concentration indicated low vitamin status. A double-blind randomized trial allocated vitamin D or placebo to adults with low vitamin status and obesity, providing 2000 IU daily in the vitamin arm. Insulin was the primary endpoint measured after fasting at entry and completion; calcium and glucose were secondary safety and metabolic measurements. Calcium concentrations did not show a clinically relevant between-group shift, and fasting glucose was 1.2 mg/dL lower with vitamin D with an interval spanning no difference. Median vitamin status rose by 16 ng/mL in the supplemented group, while recorded capsule use exceeded 89% and body weight changed by less than 1 kg in either group. A modest insulin response accompanied correction of low vitamin status, but the study was too short to assess diabetes onset or establish whether insulin changes persist after supplementation ends. The study addressed biochemical response in deficient adults rather than treatment of diagnosed diabetes, making the recruitment criteria central to interpretation.

article.title: Semaglutide and waist change across prospective obesity interventions
article.abstract: Individual intervention studies suggest that semaglutide changes central body size, but a pooled estimate can clarify the precision of the waist circumference response across treatment settings. Semaglutide is an incretin-mimetic medicine whose effects extend beyond glucose regulation. We synthesised prospective intervention studies reporting change in waist circumference during semaglutide treatment in adults with obesity without diabetes, restricting the analysis to a common follow-up period. Six studies contributed pretreatment and week 28 waist measurements; the review selected change within the semaglutide-treated participants rather than comparisons with a separate control group. A random-effects inverse-variance meta-analysis pooled mean changes from baseline; weight and systolic blood pressure were secondary pooled outcomes. The pooled population comprised treated participants with both scheduled waist measurements. Waist circumference decreased from pretreatment values during semaglutide treatment (pooled mean change -6.2 cm; 95% CI -7.3 to -5.1; p < .001); this finding was statistically significant. The pooled weight change was -6.8 kg and the systolic pressure change was -3.1 mmHg; removing the smallest study changed the waist estimate by less than 0.3 cm. All included studies used a tape-based waist protocol, although assessor masking was incompletely described in two reports; the limited number of studies prevented a reliable assessment of publication bias. The synthesis describes a reduction in waist circumference over 28 weeks, while uncertainty about longer-term maintenance and variation in measurement quality limit the implications for routine clinical care. Pooling changes within treated participants describes the observed course but cannot remove effects of dietary counselling, regression to the mean or other concurrent care.

article.abstract: The primary question was whether waist circumference decreased from baseline when adults with obesity but without diabetes received semaglutide alongside dietary counselling. The incretin-mimetic medicine semaglutide may alter central body size alongside changes in appetite. An Austrian prospective treatment study followed semaglutide recipients for 28 weeks; treatment continued throughout this period, with dietary counselling offered at scheduled visits. A trained observer measured waist circumference using a standard tape protocol; weight and blood pressure were secondary outcomes collected during the same assessments. A paired comparison evaluated the final waist measurement against baseline, using all participants who supplied both planned measurements. article.title: Dapagliflozin and fasting triglycerides in adults with diabetes
article.abstract: Dapagliflozin improves glycaemia through renal glucose excretion, while its short-term effects on fasting triglycerides may vary independently of the glucose response. This renal glucose-reabsorption blocker may influence lipid measurements through several indirect metabolic pathways. We investigated whether fasting triglycerides changed from baseline during dapagliflozin treatment in adults with type 2 diabetes receiving stable metformin therapy. A prospective intervention introduced dapagliflozin for fourteen weeks while maintaining metformin doses; participants continued their usual dietary and activity advice. Linear regression evaluated the within-person triglyceride change with adjustment for baseline triglycerides; fasting glucose and body weight were additional outcomes. Adults supplying pretreatment and endpoint triglyceride readings formed the analysis set. Fasting triglycerides decreased from baseline during dapagliflozin treatment. Fasting glucose fell by 18.4 mg/dL and body weight by 1.7 kg during treatment; these accompanying changes did not establish a mechanism for the triglyceride finding. The median baseline triglyceride concentration was 172 mg/dL, with an interquartile range of 139–218; severe hypoglycaemia was not recorded during the intervention. A modest triglyceride reduction accompanied treatment in this sample, but the brief follow-up and selected background therapy limit extrapolation to other regimens or to long-term lipid outcomes. The within-person analysis describes change during treatment and does not isolate a causal drug effect from concurrent changes in health behaviour or background care.

article.title: Triglyceride response to dapagliflozin added to stable metformin
article.abstract: A prospective intervention examined whether adding dapagliflozin to stable metformin changed fasting triglycerides from baseline in adults with type 2 diabetes over fourteen weeks. Dapagliflozin acts as a renal glucose-reabsorption blocker, but its lipid response is less consistently characterised. Adults began dapagliflozin while maintaining their background metformin; the report focused on metabolic changes during treatment without a separate untreated comparison group. Fasting triglycerides were measured before treatment and at fourteen weeks; body weight and fasting glucose were recorded at the same visits to characterise the broader metabolic response. A paired test evaluated the final triglyceride measurement against baseline, using participants with both planned observations and without imputing unmeasured visits. The study did not confirm a triglyceride benefit of dapagliflozin relative to baseline (P=.84); this finding was not statistically significant. Fasting glucose nevertheless fell by 16.9 mg/dL during treatment, while body weight declined by 1.5 kg; these secondary changes accompanied the glucose-lowering intervention. Baseline triglycerides had a median of 168 mg/dL, and recorded medication use exceeded 90%; no severe hypoglycaemic episode occurred during follow-up. The glycaemic and weight responses were detectable, but this study did not confirm a fasting triglyceride effect; a small lipid change remains compatible with the uncertainty of the estimate. The absence of a separate comparison group limits causal interpretation even when measurements are repeated in the same adults before and after treatment.

article.title: Orlistat against placebo for weight management in metabolic syndrome
article.abstract: The weight response to orlistat depends on both its pharmacological action and the accompanying dietary advice, making the reference intervention important when interpreting trial estimates. We compared orlistat with placebo for body weight reduction in adults with metabolic syndrome, giving identical brief dietary counselling to both randomized groups. A randomized trial enrolled adults with metabolic syndrome and assigned orlistat or placebo; both strategies included the same brief dietary counselling. Final body weight was compared between groups, with waist circumference and fasting triglycerides as secondary endpoints; calibrated scales were used for the weight measurements. Orlistat produced lower body weight than placebo (mean difference -2.8 kg; 95% CI -4.0 to -1.6). Waist circumference was 2.4 cm lower and fasting triglycerides were 8.5 mg/dL lower in the orlistat group; gastrointestinal symptoms were more common with active treatment. Counselling attendance was similar across groups, and participants reported no major difference in physical activity during the intervention; the study did not separately quantify changes in energy absorption. The placebo comparison indicates an incremental weight effect when brief counselling is held constant, rather than a comparison of orlistat with a comprehensive lifestyle programme. Identical counselling was intended to hold the behavioural component constant, although actual dietary change was not directly observed throughout the intervention.

article.title: Orlistat or intensive lifestyle support for adults with metabolic syndrome
article.abstract: We tested two alternative weight-management strategies: orlistat with brief dietary counselling and an intensive lifestyle programme without weight-loss medication. A randomized comparative trial assigned adults with metabolic syndrome to either strategy, allowing a direct comparison of the medication approach with intensive behavioural support. The lifestyle group attended weekly dietary and activity sessions, whereas the orlistat group received only brief counselling; body weight was measured using calibrated scales. The final weight difference between strategies was evaluated with waist circumference and attendance as secondary outcomes. Body weight was higher with orlistat plus brief counselling than with intensive lifestyle support. Waist circumference was 1.6 cm greater in the orlistat group, while attendance at assigned contacts was 84% for lifestyle sessions and 88% for medication review visits. Participants in both groups lost weight from their own baseline, so the positive between-strategy contrast should not be interpreted as weight gain caused by orlistat. Under these conditions, intensive lifestyle support achieved greater weight loss than the medication strategy tested; the result concerns competing programmes and is not an estimate of orlistat versus placebo. The comparison concerned two complete treatment strategies, so any difference could reflect contact frequency, behavioural support or medication rather than a single isolated component.

article.title: Liraglutide and fasting insulin in obesity without diabetes
article.abstract: Fasting insulin reflects both insulin secretion and the demand imposed by insulin resistance, so its direction of change during treatment may differ across metabolic settings. We assessed liraglutide versus placebo for fasting insulin in adults with obesity who had normal glucose tolerance and were not receiving glucose-lowering medication. A randomized trial allocated adults to liraglutide or placebo, with the same routine clinical advice in both arms; the report examined metabolic responses in the absence of diabetes. Fasting insulin was compared between the treatment groups; body weight and fasting glucose were secondary outcomes collected at the same visit. Liraglutide lowered fasting insulin relative to placebo (p=0.001); this finding was statistically significant. Body weight was 3.8 kg lower with liraglutide, and fasting glucose differed by -2.3 mg/dL; no participant developed sustained symptomatic hypoglycaemia during the intervention. The insulin decrease was similar after excluding people with poor recorded adherence, although medication use was assessed by returned pens rather than direct observation. Lower fasting insulin accompanied treatment in obesity with normal glucose tolerance, but the trial cannot distinguish reduced insulin demand from a direct alteration of pancreatic secretion. Recruitment before diabetes onset selected a distinct metabolic setting, and the direction of the insulin response cannot be generalised to reduced pancreatic secretory capacity.

article.title: Fasting insulin after liraglutide in recently diagnosed diabetes
article.abstract: A randomized trial investigated whether liraglutide altered fasting insulin in adults with low fasting insulin and recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes at entry, before any glucose-lowering treatment. The randomized trial included 94 adults receiving placebo as well as participants allocated to liraglutide; eligibility required recently diagnosed diabetes and low fasting insulin before glucose-lowering treatment. The clinical protocol enrolled adults whose initial fasting insulin was below 6 mIU/L, providing a population with limited basal secretion rather than hyperinsulinaemia accompanying uncomplicated obesity. Linear regression compared the final fasting insulin concentrations between treatments; fasting glucose and body weight were assessed as secondary outcomes. Fasting insulin was higher with liraglutide than placebo (mean difference 1.5 mIU/L; 95% CI 0.5 to 2.5). At the same visit, fasting glucose was 21.7 mg/dL lower and body weight was 2.9 kg lower in the liraglutide group, indicating that higher fasting insulin did not accompany worse glycaemia. No severe hypoglycaemic event was reported, and nausea did not generally require discontinuation; insulin measurements were performed in one laboratory with staff unaware of treatment allocation. The increase in fasting insulin occurred in recently diagnosed diabetes with low basal insulin, a setting that differs from obesity with preserved glucose tolerance; the measurements do not by themselves establish restoration of beta-cell function.
